Does a random forest predict heart disease better than logistic regression?

Applied Probability and Statistics project. Four hospital datasets from the UCI heart disease collection, 920 patients, one question: is the more flexible model measurably better?

Short answer: not detectably. On 184 held-out patients both models reach a ROC-AUC near 0.93, and two paired tests find no evidence that they differ.

How the analysis was run

  • The target is binary: any heart disease (original label above 0) versus none.
  • A stratified 80/20 train–test split with seed 42 gives 736 training and 184 test patients.
  • Zero cholesterol and blood-pressure readings were treated as missing and filled with medians learned from the training data, by hospital. Numeric features were standardized and categorical features one-hot encoded.
  • Both models were scored on the same test patients, so the comparisons are paired: an exact McNemar test for errors and a paired bootstrap for ROC-AUC.

The data and its quirks

Four hospitals contributed records. Their disease rates differ sharply, so the pooled 55.3% describes this particular mix of samples, not any wider population.

Disease prevalence by source, with 95% Wilson intervals

Zero values in the raw data

The source files code missing values as “?”, but some measurements are recorded as 0, which is not physiologically plausible for cholesterol or resting blood pressure. Every one of the 123 Switzerland cholesterol values is zero.

Descriptive statistics below keep these zeros as recorded. The modelling pipeline converts them to missing first.

Exploring the features

Numerical summaries

Mean differences are visible for age, maximum heart rate (thalach) and ST depression (oldpeak). Cholesterol runs the other way, with a lower mean in the disease group. That is probably the zeros again: Switzerland is 93.5% disease and contributes only zeros.

Do the models really differ?


A difference in test-set metrics can be luck. Both tests below ask whether the observed gap is larger than chance would produce, using the same 184 patients for both models.


McNemar’s exact test on classification errors


H0: both models have the same error probability. H1: they differ.






Only the 10 discordant patients carry information: 4 that logistic got right and the forest missed, and 6 the other way.


Full interpretation text


Paired bootstrap test on ROC-AUC


H0: AUC(logistic) = AUC(forest). H1: they differ. Resampling is stratified by class, 10,000 times, on the same patients for both models.






Full interpretation text


Failing to reject H0 is not proof that the models are equal. With 184 patients, small true differences would be hard to detect.





What the logistic model associates with disease


Odds ratios above 1 mean higher modelled odds of disease. Numeric features are standardized, so their ratios are per standard deviation. Categories are fully one-hot encoded without a reference level, so read those as regularized contrasts. Red intervals exclude 1.

    Limitations
    

      

    • Mixed hospital samples. Prevalence ranges from 36% to 93%. Pooling hides that, and results may not carry over to any single hospital.
      • 

    • Missing and zero-coded values. Cholesterol is entirely missing for one hospital, so imputation matters for that predictor.
      • 

    • One small test set. 184 patients means wide uncertainty. Another split could shift the metrics.
      • 

    • Association, not causation. Only 3 of 28 odds-ratio intervals exclude 1, and no multiplicity adjustment was made.
      • 

    • Not a clinical tool. This is a statistical comparison on historical data.
      • 

    

    All numbers on this page are read directly from the project’s results files. Data: UCI Heart Disease collection (Cleveland, Hungarian, Switzerland, VA Long Beach).
